claims.text: The onset and progression of premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed jointly by nanoscale size effects and Cu surface segregation.
Higher surface-to-volume ratios in smaller nanoparticles depress the melting temperature through the Gibbs–Thomson effect.
Smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles more readily segregate Cu to their surfaces.
Cu surface enrichment lowers the local melting temperature.
Cu is a lower-melting constituent of the FeNiCrCoCu alloy.
A Cu-rich surface layer reduces the cohesive energy required for premelting.
Premelting initiates at the Cu-rich surface and propagates inward toward the particle core.
Particles that are smaller and have pronounced Cu surface enrichment will have a lower premelting onset temperature than particles with suppressed surface segregation.
Particles with pronounced Cu surface enrichment will exhibit a more gradual melting transition.
The naturally Cu-segregated batch will show a statistically significant leftward shift of thermal-transition peaks relative to the passivated batch.
Mild oxidation, passivation, or mobility-limiting annealing can suppress Cu surface segregation without altering bulk composition or other relevant particle properties.
Broader particle-size distributions with minimal preferential Cu surface segregation are typical when controlled synthesis or post-synthesis treatment is absent.
DSC, XRD, and TEM-based analysis can be used during nanoparticle heating to assess thermal transitions and structural evolution.
TEM coupled with EDS can determine the surface Cu distribution needed to correlate segregation with melting behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies under inert-atmosphere heating for FeNiCrCoCu particles in the 5–20 nm size range.
Outside the specified atmosphere or size range, changes in chemistry or defect structure may cause other mechanisms to dominate.

contradictions.description: The controlled experiment specifies two batches with identical narrow size distributions and variation only in surface Cu enrichment, but the predicted outcome and baseline also invoke a comparison against a broader size distribution. This conflates size-distribution and segregation effects and does not match the stated controlled comparison.

The conditions state that only surface Cu enrichment should vary, whereas oxidation or passivation can alter surface chemistry and interfacial energetics in addition to Cu segregation. The design does not establish that these additional variables remain unchanged.
